newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO returns to Bosnia with new force.
newsitem.headline: NATO returns to Bosnia with new force.

text.p: NATO ordered a new alliance-led force into Bosnia for 18 months on Tuesday to ensure a fragile peace lasts in the war-battered country but made clear it would still not hunt down war criminals.

After months of talks and detailed planning, the alliance's 16 defence ministers approved a final "activation order" to the military to deploy a Stabilisation Force (SFOR), expected at its height to number 31,000, at a meeting in Brussels.

The new force takes over from the current Implementation Force (IFOR) policing the Dayton peace accords on December 20 -- the day its mandate expires. An official transfer of authority ceremony will be held in Sarajevo on that day.

Both NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and NATO's top commander in Europe General George Joulwan said the force would concentrate on providing the security climate in which the Dayton peace accords could continue to be implemented.

Joulwan, Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), said the force level would be reviewed every six months but the intention was to start reducing numbers once it became clear there would be no spring offensive next year.
He said he would not hesitate to call for reinforcements if he thought they were needed.
"The military can provide the secure environment, it cannot provide the peace. That must come from the people themselves," he told reporters.
He added the mission's rules of engagement were robust and said he was confident it would be able to deal with any threat.

President Bill Clinton has tentatively offered some 8,000 U.S. troops to the new force which will number between 25,000-30,000 soldiers and sees the deployment of German combat troops for the first time since World War Two.
Solana said the NATO force would not seek out and apprehend indicted war criminals, such as former Bosnian Serb leader and his former military chief Ratko Mladic.

IFOR was under instructions to detain war criminals if it came across them, but only if the local commander considered such an action would not put his men at risk. It was ordered not to actively search them out.

Solana said that position had not changed. The stand, designed to avoid allied casualties, has been widely criticised by human rights groups and international lawyers at the War Crimes Tribunal in the Hague.
"SFOR is not a police force, and therefore it is not going to be chasing war criminals, that is very clear. This is not a mission that SFOR is going to take," Solana told a news conference.
He said he supported a suggestion by U.S. General John Shalikashvili on Monday for a special police force to be set up to arrest war crimes suspects in Bosnia.
"I think that was a positive move," he said, adding that it was not yet the position of the 16-member alliance.
Shalikashvili said a separate police force should be formed to go after indicted war criminals who have not been handed over as required by the Dayton peace accords.

"I think a way must be found where a police force can be constituted that would take care in those instances where the signatories to the (agreement) continue to refuse to turn over those war criminals," he said.
SFOR, in which 17 non-NATO countries contributing to IFOR have also agreed to take part, was authorised by a U.N. Security Council resolution last week.
Russia agreed to take part after it was closely involved in planning the mission.

Five years after it refused to send troops to join the American-led coalition in the Gulf War, the German parliament approved the deployment of up to about 2,000 peacekeeping soldiers for Bosnia last Friday.
German troops took part in IFOR, but only in logistical, engineering and medical roles and they were based in Croatia. German pilots also helped enforce the "no-fly" zone over Bosnia.
